title: The lore check gate cannot detect its own staleness, so the pin silently falls behind while the gate stays green
description:
Split out of QCLI-356 on the orchestrator ruling of 2026-09-19, which chose to bump the pin now and track the detector separately rather than improvise a mechanism. Filed with the argument intact, because the one-line version of this does not carry why it matters.

THE REASONING, which is the point of the task.

lore check runs AT the pinned lore version and compares the committed schemas against what THAT version generates. So the gate is SELF-CONSISTENT BY CONSTRUCTION and stays green as the pin falls behind. Nothing inside the run can see that a newer lore exists, or that the newer lore would generate different schemas, because the only generator it ever consults is the pinned one. A green here means "the pinned version agrees with itself", and it is read as "the docs bundle is current".

This is the same shape lore-cli recorded as LCLI-504/LCLI-508, arriving a third time in this fleet: a job that installs the version a declaration names and then validates against that same declaration is a closed loop that cannot report on the declaration.

WHAT IT ALREADY COST, so the cost is not hypothetical. The pin sat at lore 0.7.0, which has NO schema-drift detection at all -- proved by deliberately corrupting a committed schema and watching 0.7.0 exit 0 with zero errors while 0.8.0 caught it. A REQUIRED context on main reported success for that entire period on a class it could not represent. The lived cost was a session unable to satisfy its own definition of done on a clean checkout, which trains people to ignore the local signal; that is the expensive part, not the drift itself.

THE CONSTRAINT ON ANY SOLUTION, and it rules out the obvious one. A detector must compare the pin against something OUTSIDE the run. It must NOT do that with a network read inside the lore check job: that job is a required context gating promotion, and a flaky required check is worse than a stale one because it teaches people to re-run until green, which destroys the signal permanently rather than narrowing it. Ruled out explicitly by opum-agent on 2026-09-19 rather than merely not chosen.

Note also that candidate-pin.json, named in the original routing as the mechanism to read, is opum-cli-e2e file in opum-cli-e2e repository. It does not exist here and there is nothing to read. That was withdrawn by the orchestrator as an object-identity error; it is recorded here only so the next reader does not go looking for it.

CANDIDATE SHAPES, none chosen, listed so the next session does not start cold:
- A scheduled (not PR-gating) job that compares the pinned number against the newest published lore and opens or comments rather than failing. Keeps the network read out of the required path.
- A release-time checklist item, which is weaker than a check and is what the two-step bump order in the workflow comment currently leans on.
- A pin file written by whatever process already knows the paired version, if such a process exists in this repository -- unverified, and worth checking before building anything.

The two-step bump order (regenerate schemas, THEN move the number) is already documented in the workflow header as of QCLI-356 and is not part of this task.

acceptanceCriteria.text: Something outside the lore check run reports when the pinned lore version is behind the newest published one, so the pin falling behind is visible without anyone remembering to look
The detector does not add a network read to the lore check job or to any other required context gating promotion, since a flaky required check is worse than a stale one
The detector distinguishes a pin that is merely behind from a pin that is behind AND would change schema generation, because only the second needs the two-step regenerate-then-bump dance
Whatever is built is proved in both directions as separate measurements: it stays quiet when the pin is current, and reports when the pin is deliberately made stale
The reasoning for why the gate cannot self-detect survives in the repository rather than only in this task, so a future reader who deletes the detector understands what they are removing
